name: Patriot (American Revolution)
summary: The Patriots were the colonists in the Thirteen Colonies who resisted British rule and then backed independence. The sources describe them as heirs of English Whig and 'country' republican thought: they stressed rights as Englishmen, then natural rights, rejected taxation without representation, and held that self-government needs virtue and constant vigilance against concentrated power. They were a broad coalition, with republican-minded gentry on one side and more democratic, agrarian and artisan groups on the other.
scope: The political ideas of the colonists who sided with the American Revolution, c. 1763-1783 (Patriots, called Whigs, Congress-men or Americans at the time), as the Yawp, Marina's Liberty Fund essay, Bailyn's account and the Perlego-excerpted scholarship describe them: radical or 'patriot' Whig and country-party republicanism, Enlightenment natural rights, and the resistance-to-independence case. It excludes Loyalists, and the later US Patriot-movement and Tea-Party-style uses of the word, and the earlier British 'patriots' opposed to Walpole. Texts tied to it: Washington's Farewell Address, as the text of a key figure.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Marina (s4, section on the end of the Revolution) quotes John Adams's hope for 'an empire of liberty... without one noble or one king among them'; the Yawp (ch. 5, section VI) says postwar society became 'less aristocratic and more meritocratic'.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Common Sense gives government the duty to protect all conscientious believers and no other business with religion; punishing a change of belief is outside that.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address urges using public credit 'as sparingly as possible' and 'avoiding likewise the accumulation of debt'; stimulus is not discussed.

collective-defense.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address rejects permanent alliances and warns against being drawn into the quarrels of others, allowing only temporary alliances for emergencies.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Patriots rejected subordinate colonial status: they argued for equal status with the mother country and the Declaration lists the cutting-off of their trade and taxation without consent as grievances.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration, quoted in the Yawp (ch. 5, section V), grounds government in 'the consent of the governed'; Daniel Dulany's 1765 'the subject shall not be taxed without his consent' and Franklin's 'prime Maxim of all free Government' (section III) show the Patriots held it, rejecting 'virtual representation' as a 'monstrous idea'.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Yawp (ch. 5, section VI) describes Massachusetts's 1780 constitution as drafted by a convention of 312 town-elected delegates, with town meetings debating the draft, as a 'more popular process of ratification'.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: The Stamp Act Congress's Declaration of Rights and Grievances claimed trial by jury as a right of Britons, resented its abridgment by the Sugar Act (Yawp ch. 5, section III), and the Continental Congress listed it among rights; the sources don't state a constitutional guarantee as such.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Washington holds the existing Constitution binding until changed by an explicit act of the people, and urges reciprocal checks and no change by usurpation.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Washington says attachment of a small nation to a great one dooms it to be a satellite, and Common Sense calls it absurd for a continent to be governed by an island.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Washington warns against the spirit of party, saying in governments purely elective it is a spirit not to be encouraged.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Common Sense devotes a section to attacking monarchy and hereditary succession as unjustified by equal natural rights or scripture.

elective-rulers.rationale: Common Sense rejects hereditary kingship and proposes that Congress choose a president by ballot.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address: 'It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world', trusting temporary alliances 'for extraordinary emergencies' only.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Yawp (ch. 5, section VI) says a number of states followed Virginia in including a bill of rights 'designed to protect the rights of individuals and circumscribe the prerogative of the government'; it doesn't say how hard it was to amend.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration's 'all men are created equal' (Yawp ch. 5, section V) and the colonists' claim to the equal rights of Britons; Marina describes the 'equalitarian' idea of equality before the law as a revolutionary mentality. But the Yawp notes it did not extend to women or the enslaved, so +1.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address urges 'good faith and justice towards all nations' and warns that passionate attachments betray a nation 'into a participation in the quarrels and wars of the latter'.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Common Sense calls the English constitution's union of king, peers and commons checking one another 'farcical' and rejects its hereditary elements as contributing nothing to freedom.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Patriots broke with the Crown and, as Marina quotes John Adams (s4), looked to freemen 'without one noble or one king among them'; the Declaration case in the Yawp (ch. 5, section V) is against the king's rule. The sources give no support for a ceremonial monarch.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address: 'religion and morality are indispensable supports' of political prosperity and 'let us with caution indulge the supposition that morality can be maintained without religion'.

more-religion-public.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address calls religion and morality indispensable supports of political prosperity and says national morality cannot be expected to prevail without religious principle.

nation-first.rationale: Washington advises as little political connection as possible with other nations and no permanent alliances, and Paine urges no partial connection with Europe, both on grounds of national interest.

national-church-status.rationale: Common Sense limits government's business with religion to protecting all conscientious believers, which leaves no room for a favoured church.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Marina (s4) says the Country Whigs opposed the statism of the Court Party, whose officials used government in economic development 'and incidentally help themselves'; the Yawp (ch. 5, section III) notes colonists resented the East India Company's Tea Act monopoly.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Washington says the right to establish government presupposes each individual's duty to obey it, and that the Constitution is sacredly obligatory until changed by the whole people.

one-party-rule.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address warns against the 'spirit of party', says the 'alternate domination of one faction over another' is 'a frightful despotism', and that a party's will should not replace 'the delegated will of the nation'.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address urges 'vigorous exertion in time of peace to discharge the debts which unavoidable wars may have occasioned, not ungenerously throwing upon posterity the burden which we ourselves ought to bear'.

people-in-arms.rationale: Split within the coalition: Marina (s4, 'Militia vs. Standing Army and Empire') says radical Whiggism held that a standing army threatened liberty and leaned to a people's militia, while the less radical members thought along conventional military lines and wanted an organised army; Washington's Farewell Address calls 'overgrown military establishments' inauspicious to liberty yet keeps 'a respectable defensive posture'.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The Patriots took up arms and the Yawp (ch. 5) reports popular violence by the Sons of Liberty as part of resistance; Marina frames the Revolution as a people's war. No general doctrine of violence is stated, so +1.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Colonists objected to smugglers being tried 'by vice-admiralty courts and not juries' and held that rights as Englishmen, including jury trial, could not be abridged (Yawp ch. 5, section III); the Yawp (section VI) also notes the new written constitutions circumscribed the prerogative of government.

property-franchise.rationale: The sources report the coalition divided: Pennsylvania's radical 1776 constitution let all free men vote 'including those who did not own property', while land remained the key to participation and other state constitutions only moderately increased the electorate (Yawp ch. 5, sections II and VI); Marina says artisans resented disenfranchisement.

property-fundamental.rationale: Washington says government must maintain all in secure enjoyment of the rights of person and property, and asks where security for property would be without religious obligation.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Declaration lists the king's obstruction of naturalization and migration as a grievance, and Common Sense calls America the asylum of persecuted lovers of liberty from every part of Europe.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Patriots resisted Parliament and the Crown as violating 'the English constitution' (Dulany, Stamp Act Congress's Declaration of Rights and Grievances, Yawp ch. 5 section III) and the Declaration (section V) affirms a right to throw off government that becomes destructive of rights.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Declaration says it is the people's right and duty to throw off despotic government, and the signers pledge their lives, fortunes and sacred honor.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Common Sense limits government's role in religion to protecting all conscientious professors, so it does not license restricting conversion.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: The Declaration of Independence as quoted in the Yawp (ch. 5, section V): 'it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish' a government destructive of rights; Marina's essay treats the Revolution as a 'people's war' and a true social revolution as well as a colonial rebellion.

right-to-secede.rationale: The Declaration (Yawp ch. 5, section V) asserts the people's right to abolish a government and institute a new one, as the colonies separated from Britain; but Washington's Farewell Address calls the unity of government 'a main pillar' of independence and liberty, and warns against those who 'weaken its bands'.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Marina says the Country Whigs understood the virtue of agrarian life, a nation of independent yeomen.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Common Sense calls the title 'sacred Majesty' applied to a king impious.

separate-church-state.rationale: Common Sense says government's only business with religion is to protect all conscientious professors of it.

separated-powers.rationale: The Yawp (ch. 5, section VI) reports that Massachusetts's 1780 constitution set up 'a three-branch government based on checks and balances'; Washington's Farewell Address warns against encroachment of one department on another and holds 'reciprocal checks' by 'dividing and distributing' power essential.

single-common-good.rationale: The Yawp describes the republican ideology as requiring those who govern to be virtuous, putting the public good over their own self-interest.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Declaration brands a king who overrides laws and charters a tyrant unfit to rule a free people, and Common Sense proposes that 'in America THE LAW IS KING'.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Radical Whigs favoured a people's militia, 'reflected later in the Second Amendment' (Marina, s4), and the Yawp (ch. 5, section III) shows the war starting when British troops marched to seize local militias' arms at Lexington and Concord.

state-harmful.rationale: Common Sense calls government a necessary evil whose end is freedom and security, and Washington calls a government of vigor indispensable to liberty; neither would abolish it.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address holds the country had 'a right to take, and was bound in duty and interest to take, a neutral position' in the European war and urges a policy of keeping out of European quarrels.

strong-leader.rationale: Washington's Farewell Address warns that 'the spirit of encroachment tends to consolidate the powers of all the departments in one' creating 'a real despotism', and that faction ends in 'the absolute power of an individual'; the Yawp (ch. 5, section VI) says the new states created weak governors.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Common Sense says government has no business with religion beyond protecting every conscientious professor of it.

taxation-theft.rationale: Patriots held that the subject may be taxed with his own consent through elected representatives, and Washington says revenue requires taxes and urges acquiescence in measures to raise it.

universal-morality.rationale: The Declaration holds as self-evident truths that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Marina (s4, section on equality in English and American Whig thought) says the republican paradigm tied virtue to equality and corruption to inequality, and the Country-Whig yeomen were 'disenchanted with the long-range corruption of a state financial system based upon great extremes of wealth'.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Marina (s4) describes the 'yeoman freeholder' model of the Country ideology, 'the apparent political stability of a nation of independent yeomen', as the appeal of the revolutionary coalition's most representative group; the Yawp (ch. 5, section II) notes land made wide participation possible.

notes: Key works left empty: no defining source I saved names a founding text together with the Patriots in a passage a validator would accept. Statements not answered (section 1-2 only).
